subsection: 10. Case study: Haussmann's Paris, and city planning

notes.b: In the nineteenth century cities grew far faster than their streets, housing and services, and governments began to see that growth could no longer be left to chance. Several pressures pushed rulers towards planning.
points: Overcrowding: industrialisation and migration from the countryside brought millions into cities, so existing streets, housing, water supplies and drainage could not cope. People crowded into the old centres to be near work, in tall, decaying houses.
Disease: with no proper drainage and polluted water, epidemics spread, and municipal authorities were slow to provide clean water and sewers. Cholera struck Paris in 1832 and 1849.

Most people blamed cholera on foul air, called miasma (bad air thought to rise from dirt and stagnant water). Clearing slums, letting in light and air, and carrying sewage away therefore seemed the cure, even before germ theory.
Fire: timber-framed, crowded housing in the older districts made fire a constant danger, and wider streets allowed fire engines to reach the buildings.
Traffic: narrow, winding medieval streets could not carry growing traffic or link the new railway stations, and they were dangerous for pedestrians and for the carriages of the wealthy.

Revolution and order: the Paris crowd overthrew governments in July 1830 and February 1848, and the June Days of 1848 were fought behind barricades. Barricades went up quickly in narrow streets, whereas wide streets let troops move.
Prestige and the economy: grand streets, public buildings and open spaces displayed the power of the state, and public works gave employment and drew investment.
notes.tip: Exams ask why planning was needed. Name all four pressures (overcrowding, disease, traffic, revolution) and give a fact for each; answers that discuss only Paris lose marks for range.

notes.b: To judge what Haussmann achieved, you need to know what he inherited: a medieval city of about one million people, crowded, unhealthy and socially divided.
points: Paris had about one million people around 1850, mostly crowded into the old centre, so the pressure on housing and services was intense.
The Île de la Cité (the island in the Seine at the heart of the city) and the area around Les Halles (the central food markets) were a maze of narrow, dark streets with poor drainage and old houses.
The Hôtel-Dieu, the main hospital on the Île de la Cité, was overcrowded and its wards were in poor conditions, which shows how badly the old centre served its people.
Water was drawn largely from the polluted Seine and the Ourcq canal, many homes had no piped water, and sewage ran into the Seine, so the city's drinking water was contaminated by its own waste.
Social geography: richer districts lay to the west, and poorer districts to the east and in the centre.

Earlier attempts: Rambuteau, Prefect of the Seine (the official in charge of Paris) from 1833 to 1848 under Louis-Philippe, cut one new street, the Rue Rambuteau, and began improvements, but on a small scale.
Earlier revolutions had been fought in these narrow streets, which reinforced the case for broad avenues.
notes.tip: For a document question, recognise the title Prefect of the Seine and the old centre of narrow streets; say why a writer might want them demolished.

notes.h: Napoleon III's aims and the London model
notes.b: The rebuilding of Paris was the project of Napoleon III, who needed the capital to show off his regime. Here are his aims and where his ideas came from.
points: Background: Louis-Napoleon took power by the coup of 2 December 1851 and the Second Empire was proclaimed in December 1852. As an authoritarian ruler who needed prestige, prosperity and order, he could override local opposition to the works.
Health: he wanted light, air, clean water and drainage for the city, in line with the belief that foul air caused disease.
Traffic and order: he wanted links between the railway stations and room for troops, so fewer barricades could be built. Employment was a further aim, through public works.
Prestige: he wanted Paris to be the showcase of the Empire, and it hosted the Universal Exhibitions of 1855 and 1867.
London was a model: during his exile there (1846-48) Louis-Napoleon admired its parks and squares, which later shaped the parks of Paris.
He gave Haussmann a map with the new streets he wanted marked in colour. Haussmann then worked out the details and greatly extended the plan, so it was not the Emperor's design alone.
notes.tip: Examiners reward linking each aim to evidence later: health to Belgrand, traffic to the boulevards and stations, order to military value, prestige to the 1867 Exhibition.

notes.b: Napoleon III needed a forceful administrator to carry out his ideas. He found one in Georges-Eugène Haussmann, and the law gave him powers to match.
points: Haussmann was born in Paris in 1809 into a Protestant family of Alsatian origin. He was a career prefect in the provinces, last at Bordeaux (the Gironde), and the Interior Minister Persigny chose him as a forceful administrator.
He was appointed Prefect of the Seine (the official in charge of Paris and its department) on 22 June 1853 and served until January 1870, working directly with the Emperor.
He was made a senator in 1857. He called himself Baron Haussmann, but Napoleon III never formally created him a baron.
The expropriation law of 1841 (compulsory purchase of property for public works) was widened by a decree of 1852. The city could buy whole plots beside a new street, so whole blocks could be cleared.

Methods were centralised: control lay with the Prefect and the Emperor, and the Prefecture of the Seine had large budgets and a large team of engineers and architects, including Belgrand and Alphand. Much of the money was borrowed outside parliamentary control.
Building regulations fixed the heights and facades of buildings along the new streets, so the city's look could be controlled.
notes.tip: Do not say the Emperor made Haussmann a baron. Remember the dates: Prefect from June 1853 to January 1870; the 1841 law and the 1852 decree gave him the legal power to clear blocks.

notes.h: The boulevards and the grands travaux
notes.b: The grands travaux (great works) were the programme of demolition and rebuilding that Haussmann directed from 1853, carried out in stages. Its core was a network of new straight avenues cut through the old city.
points: The grande croisée (great crossing) was an east-west axis, the Rue de Rivoli, extended eastwards in the 1850s, crossed by a north-south axis of the Boulevard de Strasbourg (begun 1852), the Boulevard de Sébastopol (opened 1858) and then the Boulevard Saint-Michel on the Left Bank.
This crossing linked the Seine to the railway stations to the north, so it solved a traffic problem as well as clearing the old centre.

The Boulevard Saint-Germain on the Left Bank and the Avenue de l'Opéra were completed in the 1870s, under the Third Republic. The Avenue de l'Impératrice (now Avenue Foch) was laid out in 1854 as the route to the Bois de Boulogne.
Twelve avenues radiate from the Place de l'Étoile, which became a great star-shaped junction. The Avenue de l'Opéra was designed to frame the view of the new Opéra.

The design: long straight streets with vistas ending on a monument, lined with trees, pavements, gas lamps, benches and kiosks, and with uniform cream stone apartment facades of controlled height (the Haussmann building).
The Île de la Cité was largely cleared of housing and rebuilt with public buildings, including the rebuilt Hôtel-Dieu, the law courts and police headquarters.

The boulevards served several purposes: traffic and access to the stations, light and air, and a military argument, since troops and artillery could move along wide straight streets and barricades were harder to hold.
Haussmann himself stressed health and traffic over the military motive, which is worth remembering when judging his aims.
notes.tip: The Rue de Rivoli extension was decided before Haussmann arrived, so say it was extended eastwards in the 1850s rather than crediting him with starting it. For short-paragraph questions, a dated fact such as the Boulevard de Sébastopol scores well.

notes.b: Wide streets alone would not cure disease, so the engineer Eugène Belgrand, in charge of water and sewers, rebuilt the city's water system underground.
points: Belgrand built aqueducts (channels carrying water over long distances) bringing spring water from the Dhuis valley, completed in 1865, and the Vanne valley, completed in 1874 after the Empire had fallen. The water went to covered reservoirs in the city, which kept it clean.
A double system supplied drinking water and non-drinking water: Seine water was kept for street cleaning and fountains, so the clean spring water was reserved for drinking.
Sewers: a large underground sewer network of tunnels, big enough to walk through, carried waste water away from the centre and out of the city downstream. It became a sight for visitors.
Effects: cleaner streets and water and better sanitation, which cut the disease that the polluted Seine had spread.
There were limits: many houses were not yet connected, and household sewage was not fully carried away until later in the century.
Parallel work in London: Bazalgette's main drainage there was begun in 1859, so the two capitals were doing similar sanitary engineering in the same years.
notes.tip: For the health aim, give Belgrand's water and sewers as the evidence, then add the limit that many houses were unconnected. Do not mix up Belgrand (water), Alphand (parks) and Haussmann (the Prefect).

notes.b: The rebuilt city also gave Parisians green space, partly on the London model. Jean-Charles Alphand, the engineer in charge of the parks and promenades, designed much of their planting and layout.
points: The Bois de Boulogne (west) was given to the city by the state in 1852 and laid out as an English-style park with lakes and paths. The Longchamp racecourse opened there in 1857.
The Bois de Vincennes (east) was laid out in the 1860s as a counterpart for the working-class eastern districts, so that east and west each had a large park.
The Buttes-Chaumont (north-east) was a former quarry and rubbish dump turned into a park with a lake, cliffs and a temple on a rocky island. It opened in 1867, the Exhibition year.
Smaller parks and squares: the Parc Monceau was redesigned, the Parc Montsouris was begun in the south, and many small neighbourhood squares gave residents green space close to home.
notes.tip: The three big parks are easily confused: Boulogne is west, wealthy and has the racecourse; Vincennes is east and serves working-class districts; Buttes-Chaumont is north-east, a former quarry. Longchamp racecourse has appeared in document questions.

notes.b: Alongside streets and parks, the works added public buildings that displayed the Empire and met practical needs.
points: The Opéra: Charles Garnier won the design competition in 1861, building began in 1862, and it opened in 1875, after the fall of the Empire. It stands as a symbol of Second Empire display.
Les Halles, the central food market, was rebuilt as iron-and-glass pavilions by Victor Baltard from the 1850s, the first iron pavilions dating from 1854. The pavilions were demolished in 1971.
Railway stations: the Gare du Nord was rebuilt in the 1860s (architect Jacques Hittorff), and the new boulevards linked the stations to the centre and to each other.
Street furniture and fountains: Gabriel Davioud designed kiosks, lamps and benches, and the Saint-Michel fountain (1860). These gave the new streets a uniform appearance.
Other buildings included churches, town halls for the arrondissements (the districts of Paris), schools, barracks and the new Hôtel-Dieu.
notes.tip: Match each architect to the building: Garnier (Opéra), Baltard (Les Halles), Davioud (street furniture). Opéra questions expect you to know that it opened only in 1875, under the Third Republic.

notes.b: By the late 1850s Paris had spilled beyond its old customs wall. Annexing the suburbs let Haussmann plan the whole urban area.
points: On 1 January 1860, under a law of 1859, the communes (local districts) between the old customs wall and the fortifications were annexed to the city, and the number of arrondissements rose from twelve to twenty.
The annexed communes included both working-class districts (Belleville, Montmartre) and richer ones such as Passy, a well-off western district.
The city grew to about 1.7 million people at the 1861 census, and to about 1.8 million by the late 1860s.
Why: to plan the whole urban area, to extend the boulevards and services outward, and to bring the growing suburbs under the city's control and taxes.
notes.tip: Document questions have asked about the arrondissements: know that there were twelve, then twenty from 1860. Do not confuse the 1860 annexation with the 1841 law or the 1852 decree.

notes.b: The works were enormously expensive. The way Haussmann paid for them made him vulnerable once the Empire began to liberalise.
points: Financing came from state subsidies, city revenue (mainly the octroi, a tax on goods entering the city), loans, and the hope that rising property values would pay for the works, which Haussmann called productive expenditure.

Hidden borrowing: the Caisse des travaux de Paris (1858) and advance payments to contractors, the bons de délégation, let Haussmann borrow without the approval of the Legislative Body. The city's debt grew greatly in the 1860s.
Court decisions in the late 1850s and 1860s made the city pay more compensation to expropriated owners, which raised costs and helped speculators.

Jules Ferry, a republican journalist, attacked the cost and irregular borrowing in articles of 1867-68, collected as Les Comptes fantastiques d'Haussmann (1868; his pamphlet), a pun on Les Contes fantastiques d'Hoffmann.
The fall: the Empire was turning liberal and the opposition was strong in Paris after the 1869 elections, so Émile Ollivier's new ministry, formed in January 1870, dismissed Haussmann that month.

Afterwards the Third Republic finished many projects, such as the Avenue de l'Opéra and the Boulevard Saint-Germain. Haussmann published his Mémoires (three volumes, 1890-93) defending his work, and died in 1891.
He accepted the label artiste démolisseur (demolition artist) for himself.
notes.tip: Do not confuse his dismissal (January 1870, by Ollivier's liberal ministry) with the fall of the Empire (September 1870, after Sedan). For the cost, say 'huge debt' with no figure.

notes.b: The rebuilding changed who could live where in Paris. Its benefits went mainly to the wealthy, while its costs fell on the poor.
points: Displacement: demolition destroyed many cheap central houses, so working-class families were pushed out to the east, the north and the annexed suburbs, often further from their work.
Rents rose in the rebuilt centre, and the new apartment blocks suited the middle classes.
The east-west divide sharpened: a wealthy west, with the Bois de Boulogne, and a working-class east, with districts such as Belleville and Ménilmontant.
Speculation: property developers and financiers made fortunes from rising land values. Émile Zola's novel La Curée (serialised 1871, book 1872) portrayed this speculation.
Employment: the works employed large numbers of building workers, many of them migrants from the provinces, though much work was seasonal.

Political effect: displaced workers in the east became a base for radical and republican politics in Belleville (Gambetta's Belleville programme, 1869). The Paris Commune of March-May 1871 showed barricades were still possible, though the army retook the city in the Bloody Week of May 1871.
notes.tip: Zola's La Curée is about speculation and the rich, not the east-west divide. Use displacement, rents and the divide as the social costs when judging success.

notes.b: Critics attacked Haussmann's Paris from several directions: cost, loss of the old city, and social exclusion. Defenders replied that it brought health, jobs and beauty.
points: Victor Hugo had campaigned long before Haussmann against the destruction of old buildings, in his 'War on the demolishers' (written 1825, published again 1832), and in Notre-Dame de Paris (1831), which celebrated medieval Paris.

Hugo was in exile from December 1851 to September 1870, opposing Napoleon III, so he was abroad for the whole period of the works. He did not write a specific attack on them; his writing stood for the old Paris that Haussmann destroyed.
Writers mourned the old Paris: Charles Baudelaire's poem 'Le Cygne' (The Swan), published 1860 and in Les Fleurs du mal from the 1861 edition, and the journal of Edmond and Jules de Goncourt.
Political critics: republicans and liberals such as Jules Ferry and Adolphe Thiers attacked the cost, the debt and the lack of control by elected bodies.

Other criticisms: the uniform facades and straight lines were monotonous, historic buildings and neighbourhoods were destroyed, the poor were excluded from the new city, and the boulevards were seen as built for troops.
Defenders: Haussmann and the Emperor pointed to health, traffic, beauty, jobs and prestige, and visitors to the 1867 Exhibition admired the new city.
notes.tip: Do not claim Hugo wrote a specific attack on Haussmann's works, and do not quote him. Match the critic to the criticism: Ferry (finance, 1868), Zola (speculation), Baudelaire (loss of old Paris, 1860), Hugo (defence of old Paris).

notes.b: Paris was the most dramatic case, but other cities also tackled growth, and comparing them shows what was distinctive about Haussmann's method.
points: Vienna: Emperor Franz Joseph's decree of December 1857 ordered the old city walls demolished and replaced by the Ringstrasse, a broad ring boulevard lined with public buildings (parliament, town hall, university, opera, museums) and apartment blocks. It opened in 1865 and was mostly finished later.
Plots along the Ringstrasse were sold to private builders, whose purchases paid for much of it.
Barcelona: Ildefons Cerdà's plan of 1859 for extending the city, the Eixample, set out a regular grid of blocks with cut-off corners, so it expanded outward rather than cutting through the old town.

Brussels: the River Senne was covered over and central boulevards built (1867-71) under the burgomaster Jules Anspach, partly on the Paris model. In Berlin James Hobrecht drew up a plan for the city's expansion in 1862.

British sanitary reform: The sanitary reform movement of the 1840s, led by Edwin Chadwick and others, produced his sanitary report (1842) and the Public Health Act (1848), which pressed for drainage and public health.
London's Great Stink of summer 1858 led Joseph Bazalgette of the Metropolitan Board of Works to build main sewers from 1859, with the Victoria Embankment (1870) along the Thames.

Contrast: Paris was planned from above by an authoritarian state with power over property, whereas British cities relied mainly on local authorities and permissive laws, improving drains and water more than street plans.
notes.tip: Planning questions need at least one other example beside Paris: Vienna's Ringstrasse (replaced walls, 1857), Barcelona's Eixample (a grid, 1859) or British sanitary reform. Keep them distinct from Haussmann's cutting through an existing city.

notes.b: Haussmann's work outlived the Empire and has been judged very differently since.
points: Haussmannisation became a term for large-scale clearance and boulevard planning, and it was copied in French cities and abroad.
Admirers see the creator of modern Paris and a pioneer of modern city planning and public health.
Critics see a destroyer of old Paris and a planner who served the regime, the wealthy and speculators and pushed the poor to the edges.
Lasting features: most of central Paris's street plan, apartment blocks, parks and sewers still date from his works, though Baltard's Les Halles pavilions were demolished in the early 1970s.

notes.h: Assessment: success and failure of Haussmann's Paris
notes.b: A good judgement of Haussmann weighs each aim against the evidence, then sets the costs against the achievements. The verdict is largely successful in physical and sanitary terms, less so socially and financially.
points: Success on health: water, sewers, light and air largely achieved, because Belgrand's aqueducts and sewers cleaned the city. Failure: it was not complete by 1870, since many houses were still unconnected.
Success on traffic and stations: the boulevards linked the Seine and the railway stations, so movement was transformed.
Order: barricades were harder to build but not prevented, as the Commune of 1871 showed, so this aim was only partly achieved.
Success on beauty and prestige: the parks, the Opéra, the uniform facades and the 1867 Exhibition made Paris a model. Jobs: many were created, but much work was seasonal.
Failure on social grounds: displacement, higher rents and the east-west divide, because rising property values meant rents and speculation as well as benefits.
Failure on cost: the destruction of historic Paris, and huge debt and irregular finance that brought his dismissal in 1870, plus speculation.
Contemporary vs later views: Ferry, Hugo's defence of old Paris and Baudelaire criticised it, but visitors in 1867 admired it, and later admirers see a pioneer of modern planning.
Comparison with Hugo, Darwin or Napoleon III: Haussmann's achievement was practical and physical, and it was lasting in the street plan and sewers.
notes.tip: Judge each aim in turn (health, traffic, order, beauty and prestige, jobs), then the limits, and finish with a clear overall verdict. A description of the works without judgement does not earn the marks.

keyTerms.definition: The great public works, such as new boulevards, parks and sewers, that Haussmann carried out in Paris from 1853.
The senior official in charge of Paris and the Seine department, a post Haussmann held from 1853 to 1870.
A wide, straight, tree-lined avenue, which Haussmann used to open up the city and to improve traffic and military movement.
The compulsory purchase of property by the state for public works, governed in France by the 1841 law.
The incorporation of the Paris suburbs into the city in 1860, which increased the number of arrondissements from twelve to twenty.
An underground channel that carries waste water away from houses and streets, which Belgrand built on a large scale in Paris.
The grand boulevard built in Vienna from 1857, replacing the old city walls with public buildings.
The organised measures to protect the health of a population, through clean water, sanitation, housing and disease control.

factCards.definition: Georges-Eugène Haussmann was born in 1809 and was appointed Prefect of the Seine in June 1853.
Haussmann was dismissed in January 1870 when the new liberal ministry of Émile Ollivier would not keep a prefect so unpopular with the opposition.
In 1860 the Paris suburbs were annexed and the city grew from twelve to twenty arrondissements.
The engineer Belgrand built aqueducts and a sewer network that brought clean water into Paris and carried waste away.
The Bois de Boulogne, on the western edge of Paris, was redesigned as a park with lakes, paths and a racecourse in the 1850s.
The former quarry in north-east Paris was transformed into a park with a lake and a cliff-top waterfall, which opened in 1867.
Charles Garnier's Paris Opéra was begun in 1861 and opened in 1875, a symbol of the imperial city.
The central food markets of Paris were rebuilt as iron-and-glass pavilions by Victor Baltard from the 1850s.
The north-south boulevard cut through the centre of Paris, linking the Seine with the northern railway stations.
The republican journalist Jules Ferry attacked the cost of Haussmann's works in a pamphlet of 1868 titled The Fantastic Accounts of Haussmann.
The decree of 1857 that began the grand boulevard around the old city of Vienna, built in the 1860s and 1870s.
Ildefons Cerdà's 1859 plan for the extension of Barcelona, with a regular grid of blocks.
